facts.fact: India lies between 8°4' N–37°6' N and 68°7' E–97°25' E.
IST is based on the 82°30' E meridian, 5 h 30 min ahead of GMT.
India is the seventh-largest country by area (3.287 million km²).
The Tropic of Cancer passes through eight Indian states.
India's longest land border is with Bangladesh (4,096 km).
Indira Point (Great Nicobar) is India's southernmost point.
Kanchenjunga is the highest peak in India.
The Himalayan ranges north to south are the Trans Himalaya, Himadri, Himachal and Shiwalik.
The Purvanchal comprises the Patkai, Naga, Manipur and Mizo (Lushai) hills.
The Northern Plains belts are Bhabar, Terai, Bhangar and Khadar from north to south.
The Peninsular Plateau, India's oldest and largest division, formed from the Gondwana landmass.
The Vindhya lies north of the Narmada; the Satpura between the Narmada and Tapi.
The Western Coastal Plain is submergent; the Eastern is emergent and wider.
Andaman & Nicobar are volcanic/tectonic islands; Lakshadweep is coral.
The Great Rann of Kutch lies in Gujarat.
The five Punjab rivers unite as the Panchnad.
The Narmada and Tapi flow west into the Arabian Sea.
An antecedent river keeps its course across a rising mountain (Indus, Brahmaputra).
The SW monsoon is driven by a low over the Tibetan Plateau and the northward shift of the STJ.
The NE (retreating) monsoon rains on the Coromandel coast and coastal Andhra Pradesh.
Black (regur) soil of the Deccan Trap is ideal for cotton.
The Sundari tree marks tidal (mangrove) forests.
Jog (Gersoppa) Falls is on the Sharavati.
AP combines the Deccan plateau margin, the Eastern Ghats and an emergent east coast.
Champion & Seth classify forests into 5 major groups and 16 type-groups.
Jim Corbett (1936) was India's first national park; Project Tiger began in 1973.
Hemis (Ladakh) is India's largest national park.
Madhya Pradesh has the most tigers.
Gir NP is the stronghold of the Asiatic lion.
The Asiatic wild ass lives in the Little Rann of Kutch.
The hangul lives in Dachigam NP.
The Godavari rises at Trimbak, the Krishna at Mahabaleshwar and the Narmada at Amarkantak.
Anaimudi, the highest peninsular peak, is in the Western Ghats; the Ghats meet in the Nilgiris.
A dendritic pattern is tree-like.
A centripetal pattern drains inward into a basin.
Bandarpunch feeds the Yamuna, Bara Shigri the Chenab, Milam the Goriganga and Siachen the Nubra.
Cardamom Hills (Western Ghats), Kaimur (Vindhya), Mahadeo (Satpura), Mikir (Assam).
The Indravati and Pranahita are Godavari tributaries; the Pennar is not a Krishna tributary.
The Nagavali and Vamsadhara rise in the Eastern Ghats.
The Ten Degree Channel separates Andaman from Nicobar; Great Nicobar is close to Sumatra.
The Western Ghats spread over six states; Pulicat over two (AP and TN); the Himalaya over more than five.
Zoji La, Khardung La, Karakoram Pass and Nathu La are key Himalayan passes.
Wular (largest freshwater), Chilika (largest lagoon), Sambhar (inland salt), Kolleru (AP freshwater).
Laterite soil suits tea/cashew; desert soil bajra; alluvial wheat–rice.
Tropical deciduous (monsoon) forests are the most widespread.
Kaziranga is the stronghold of the one-horned rhinoceros.
The 82°30' E standard meridian passes through five states: Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Odisha and Andhra Pradesh.
India spans about 30° of longitude, so local time differs by about two hours between Arunachal and Gujarat.
India has 28 states and 8 Union Territories.
India occupies about 2.4% of the world's land area.
India shares maritime boundaries with Sri Lanka and the Maldives.
Ujjain (Mahakaleshwar temple) lies close to the Tropic of Cancer.
The easternmost point of India is Kibithu in Arunachal Pradesh.
The westernmost point of India is Guhar Moti (Sir Creek area) in Kutch, Gujarat.
The southernmost point of mainland India is Kanyakumari (Cape Comorin).
Indira Col in the Karakoram (Siachen area, Ladakh) is the northernmost point of India.
Five states border Nepal: Uttarakhand, Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, West Bengal and Sikkim.
Five states border Bangladesh: West Bengal, Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram.
Four states border Myanmar: Arunachal Pradesh, Nagaland, Manipur and Mizoram.
Four states border Bhutan: Sikkim, West Bengal, Assam and Arunachal Pradesh.
China borders Ladakh, Himachal Pradesh, Uttarakhand, Sikkim and Arunachal Pradesh.
Pakistan borders Gujarat, Rajasthan, Punjab, Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh.
The Palk Strait and Gulf of Mannar separate India from Sri Lanka.
India is larger than the European Union but smaller than Russia, Canada, the USA, China, Brazil and Australia.
Mount Everest (8,848 m) lies in Nepal and is the world's highest peak.
K2 / Godwin-Austen (8,611 m) in the Karakoram is the highest peak of Indian territory as claimed (in PoK/Gilgit-Baltistan).
Kanchenjunga (8,586 m) on the Sikkim–Nepal border is the highest peak in India and the third-highest in the world.
Nanda Devi (7,816 m) in the Kumaon–Garhwal Himalaya is the highest peak lying wholly within India.
Nanga Parbat (8,126 m) is the western anchor of the Great Himalaya (Gilgit-Baltistan).
Namcha Barwa (7,782 m) marks the eastern end of the Himalaya at the great bend of the Tsangpo, just beyond Arunachal.
Kamet (7,756 m) is a high peak of the Garhwal Himalaya, Uttarakhand.
Makalu (8,481 m), Dhaulagiri (8,172 m) and Annapurna (8,078 m) are Great Himalayan peaks in Nepal.
Saramati (3,826 m) in the Naga Hills is the highest peak of Nagaland.
Phawngpui (Blue Mountain, about 2,157 m) is the highest peak of Mizoram.
Shillong Peak (1,961 m) is the highest point of the Meghalaya plateau; Nokrek (1,412 m) is the highest of the Garo Hills.
Anamudi (2,695 m) in the Anaimalai Hills (Eravikulam NP, Kerala) is the highest peak of peninsular India.
Doddabetta (2,637 m) is the highest peak of the Nilgiri Hills, Tamil Nadu.
Mullayanagiri (1,930 m) in the Baba Budan Hills is the highest peak of Karnataka.
Kalsubai (1,646 m) is the highest peak of the northern Western Ghats (Sahyadri, Maharashtra).
Guru Shikhar (1,722 m) at Mount Abu is the highest peak of the Aravalli range.
Dhupgarh (1,350 m) near Pachmarhi is the highest peak of the Satpura range.
The Vindhya range rises only to about 752 m (Kalumar/Sad-bhawna peak).
Arma Konda / Jindhagada (about 1,680 m) in Andhra Pradesh is the highest peak of the Eastern Ghats.
Mahendragiri (1,501 m) in Odisha is the highest peak of the northern Eastern Ghats (the source text calls it the highest of all).
Agasthyamalai (Agasthyakoodam, 1,868 m) is a southern Western Ghats peak on the Kerala–Tamil Nadu border.
The Himalaya stretch about 2,500 km east–west, about 400 km wide in Kashmir and 150 km in Arunachal.
The Himadri has an average height of about 6,000 m, asymmetric folds and a granite core.
The Lesser Himalaya (Himachal) is 3,700–4,700 m high and about 50 km wide, made of highly compressed rocks.
The Shiwalik is 10–15 km wide and 900–1,100 m high, made of unconsolidated river gravels.
Duns are longitudinal valleys between the Shiwalik and Lesser Himalaya — Dehra Dun (largest), Kotli Dun, Patli Dun.
Karewas are thick glacial clay and moraine deposits of the Kashmir Himalaya used for saffron (zafran) cultivation.
The Kashmir Valley lies between the Great Himalaya and the Pir Panjal; the Ladakh cold desert lies between the Great Himalaya and the Karakoram.
The Himachal–Uttarakhand Himalaya run from the Ravi in the west to the Kali (a Ghaghara tributary) in the east.
The Lesser Himalaya are called the Dhauladhar in Himachal Pradesh and the Nagtibba in Uttarakhand.
The Darjeeling–Sikkim Himalaya lack the Shiwalik; their Duar formations were developed by the British for tea.
The Arunachal Himalaya run from Bhutan to the Diphu Pass; Kangtu and Namcha Barwa are its peaks.
Subansiri, Kameng, Dihang, Dibang and Lohit cross the Arunachal Himalaya in deep gorges with great hydel potential.
The Purvanchal hills are made mainly of sandstone (sedimentary rock) and run as parallel ranges south of the Dihang gorge.
Jammu Dun and Pathankot Dun lie in the southern Kashmir Himalaya.
Zoji La (Great Himalaya, near Dras) links Srinagar with Kargil and Leh; a Zojila tunnel is under construction since 2020.
Banihal Pass (Pir Panjal) carries the Jammu–Srinagar route, now bypassed by the Jawahar Tunnel.
The Pir Panjal Pass carries the historic Mughal Road between Rajouri and the Kashmir Valley.
Burzil Pass connects the Astore valley with the Deosai plains.
Pensi La (Great Himalaya) links the Suru valley/Kargil with Zanskar.
Khardung La (Ladakh range) is the gateway to the Nubra valley and the Siachen supply route.
Chang La links Leh with Pangong Lake.
Umling La (about 19,000 ft, opened 2021) is the highest motorable pass in India.
Taglang La (5,328 m) on the Manali–Leh road links Debring with Gya.
Bara-lacha La (Zanskar range) links Lahaul with Leh on the Manali–Leh route; the Chenab rises near it.
Imis La links Ladakh with Tibet towards the Hanle valley.
Lanak La in Aksai Chin connects Ladakh with Lhasa.
The Karakoram Pass links Ladakh with China (Xinjiang) across the Karakoram range.
Aghil Pass, north of K2 (Godwin-Austen), links Ladakh with Xinjiang.
Shipki La (Sutlej gorge) links Kinnaur, Himachal Pradesh, with Tibet and is a trade post with China.
Rohtang Pass links the Kullu valley with Lahaul–Spiti; the Atal Tunnel (2020) bypasses it.
Debsa Pass links the Kullu (Parvati) and Spiti valleys.
Lipulekh (Uttarakhand) at the India–Nepal–Tibet tri-junction is the Kailash–Mansarovar Yatra route.
Mana Pass (Uttarakhand, Nanda Devi BR) links Mana village with Tibet.
Niti Pass, an old Uttarakhand–Tibet route, has been closed since 1962.
Traill's Pass links the Pindari glacier valley with the Milam valley.
Mangsha Dhura (Kuthi valley) is another Uttarakhand–Tibet pilgrim pass.
Muling La is a seasonal pass north of Gangotri into Tibet.
Nathu La (Sikkim) is an India–China trade pass, reopened for trade in 2006 on the old Silk Route.
Jelep La (Sikkim) runs through the Chumbi valley to Lhasa; closed after 1962.
Bomdi La (Arunachal, east of Bhutan) links Arunachal Pradesh with Lhasa.
Diphu Pass on the McMahon Line marks the India–China–Myanmar tri-junction.
Pangsau Pass (about 3,727 ft) gives Arunachal Pradesh one of the easiest routes into Myanmar (Stilwell Road).
Dihang Pass (over 4,000 m) links Arunachal Pradesh with Mandalay, Myanmar.
Bhor Ghat (Khandala) carries the Mumbai–Pune rail and road; the Satavahanas used it to link Konkan ports with the Deccan.
Thal Ghat (Kasara) carries the Mumbai–Nashik road and rail.
The Palghat (Palakkad) Gap between the Nilgiri and Anaimalai hills links Coimbatore with Palakkad.
The Shencottah Gap links Madurai (Tamil Nadu) with Kottayam/Kollam (Kerala).
The Peninsular Plateau is bounded by the Delhi Ridge (NW), Rajmahal hills (E), Gir range (W) and Cardamom hills (S).
The north-west of the plateau has the Chambal ravines (Bhind, Morena) — badlands formed by gully erosion.
The Central Highlands narrow eastward as Bundelkhand, Baghelkhand and the mineral-rich Chotanagpur plateau.
The Malwa plateau (500–700 m) is a basaltic lava plateau with black soil drained by the Chambal, Mahi and Narmada.
Bundelkhand lies between the Yamuna and the Vindhya, drained by the Betwa and Ken.
Central Highland rivers — Chambal, Kali Sindh, Banas, Parbati, Betwa, Ken — flow north-east to the Yamuna, showing the plateau slopes north-east.
The Mahadeo, Kaimur and Maikal ranges are eastward extensions of the Satpura; the Deccan continues NE as the Meghalaya, Karbi-Anglong and North Cachar hills.
The Meghalaya plateau (Garo, Khasi, Jaintia hills) is separated from the main plateau by the Malda (Garo–Rajmahal) gap, a fault.
The Vindhya range is about 1,000 km long (sandstone); the Satpura about 800 km (granite, basalt).
The Vindhya forms the traditional divide between north and south India.
The Aravalli are the oldest fold mountains of India, running SW–NE from Gujarat to Delhi.
The Deccan plateau slopes gently eastward, so its main rivers flow east to the Bay of Bengal.
The Deccan includes the Maharashtra (black-soil lava), Karnataka, Telangana (granite, coal, limestone), Andhra and Tamil Nadu plateaus.
The Andhra plateau (about 500–900 m) is drained by the Godavari and Krishna and is known for bauxite and forests.
The Meghalaya plateau is known for limestone caves and very heavy monsoon erosion.
The Western Ghats are block mountains/escarpments with a steep western face (step-like "treppen") and a gentle eastern slope.
The Western Ghats run from the Tapi valley to Kanyakumari.
The Western Ghats are a UNESCO World Heritage Site (2012) and a global biodiversity hotspot.
Local names: Sahyadri (Maharashtra), Nilgiri (Karnataka–TN), Anaimalai and Cardamom hills (Kerala–TN).
The height of the Western Ghats increases from north to south.
The northern Western Ghats (Tapi to 16°N) are Deccan basalt; the central part (16°–13°N) granite and gneiss.
The Godavari, Krishna, Kaveri, Periyar and Bhavani rise in the Western Ghats.
The Western Ghats intercept the SW monsoon, giving heavy orographic rain to Kerala and the Konkan.
Western Ghats hills north→south: Satmala, Harishchandra, Baba Budan, Nilgiri, Anaimalai, Agasthyamalai, Cardamom.
The Cardamom Hills are the southernmost range of the Western Ghats (Kerala–Tamil Nadu).
The Anaimalai ("elephant mountains") hold Anamudi.
Silent Valley and Parambikulam are biodiversity highlights of the southern Western Ghats.
The Eastern Ghats are older, lower, discontinuous and cut by the Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna and Kaveri.
The Eastern Ghats are made of crystalline rocks — gneiss, granite and khondalite/charnockite.
The Eastern Ghats spread over Odisha, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Karnataka and Tamil Nadu.
The Eastern Ghats hold rich bauxite (Odisha, Andhra Pradesh) and iron ore.
The Nallamala hills (AP–Telangana) are the core of the central Eastern Ghats.
The Palkonda hills lie in the Rayalaseema region of Andhra Pradesh.
The Velikonda hills (granite ridges) run along the AP–TN side of the Eastern Ghats.
The Simhachalam and Kailasagiri hills lie near Visakhapatnam.
The Shevaroy hills (Yercaud, coffee) and Javadi hills are in Tamil Nadu.
The Western and Eastern Ghats meet in the Nilgiri Hills.
The coastal plains stretch about 6,000 km and meet at Kanyakumari.
The Kutch peninsula was once an island, joined to the mainland by Indus sediments.
The Konkan coast runs from Mumbai to Goa (Mandovi, Zuari rivers).
The Karnataka (Kanara) coast runs from Goa to Mangalore.
The Malabar coast of Kerala is known for backwaters (kayals) and lagoons such as Vembanad.
The Utkal coast is the Odisha section of the east coast, with Chilika lake.
The Northern Circars run from the Mahanadi to the Krishna delta along Odisha–Andhra Pradesh.
The Coromandel coast is the Tamil Nadu coast (Chennai–Cuddalore, Cauvery delta), extending from the Krishna to Kanyakumari in the wider sense.
West-coast rivers form estuaries; east-coast rivers form wide deltas.
The east coast has a wide continental shelf and few natural harbours (Kolkata is a riverine exception).
The west coast gets rain mainly from the SW monsoon; the east coast from both the SW and NE monsoons.
The Bengal coast holds the Sundarbans, the world's largest mangrove forest.
West-coast ports include Kandla (Deendayal), Mumbai, Mormugao, New Mangalore and Kochi.
East-coast ports include Kolkata–Haldia, Paradip, Visakhapatnam, Chennai and Tuticorin (V.O. Chidambaranar).
West-coast farming is monsoon-fed coconut, rubber and spices; east-coast deltas grow irrigated rice and sugarcane.
The Andaman and Nicobar Islands lie between about 6°45' N and 13°41' N and stretch about 590 km.
The Andaman & Nicobar group has about 572 islands (38 inhabited).
Port Blair, the A&N capital in South Andaman, was renamed Sri Vijaya Puram in 2024.
The Duncan Passage separates South Andaman from Little Andaman.
The Ten Degree Channel separates the Andaman group from the Nicobar group.
St. George's Channel separates Little Nicobar from Great Nicobar.
The Grand (Great) Channel separates Great Nicobar from Sumatra (Indonesia).
The Coco Channel separates North Andaman from Myanmar's Coco Islands.
The Nine Degree Channel separates Minicoy from the rest of Lakshadweep.
The Eight Degree Channel separates Minicoy from the Maldives.
Saddle Peak (about 732 m, North Andaman) is the highest point of the Andaman & Nicobar Islands.
Barren Island is India's only active volcano; Narcondam is a dormant volcano.
Andaman tribes: Jarawa, Sentinelese, Onge and Great Andamanese.
Nicobar tribes: the semi-nomadic Shompen and the settled Nicobarese.
Great Nicobar is the largest and southernmost Nicobar island, about 147 km from Sumatra.
Car Nicobar (northern Nicobar group) has a strategic air base.
The Nicobar pigeon is the state bird of the A&N Islands.
The A&N Islands receive about 3,000 mm of rain a year and are near the Malacca Strait.
Lakshadweep has 36 islands, only 10 inhabited, with about 32 km² of land — India's smallest UT.
Kavaratti is the capital of Lakshadweep.
The Amindivi islands are the northern group and Minicoy the southernmost island of Lakshadweep.
All Lakshadweep islands are coral atolls with fringing reefs, only 1–2 m above sea level.
Mahl, a form of Dhivehi, is spoken in Minicoy; Malayalam is widely spoken in Lakshadweep.
Pitti island of Lakshadweep is a bird sanctuary.
Andrott is the largest island of Lakshadweep by land area (the source text calls Minicoy the largest).
Majuli in the Brahmaputra (Assam) is the world's largest river island and India's first island district (2016).
Umananda (Peacock Island) near Guwahati is the smallest inhabited river island.
Abdul Kalam Island (formerly Wheeler Island) off Odisha is India's missile-testing site.
Sagar Island in the Ganga delta hosts the Ganga Sagar Mela at Makar Sankranti.
New Moore (South Talpatti) Island in the Bay of Bengal emerged after a 1970 cyclone and was disputed by India and Bangladesh.
Sriharikota (AP), India's rocket-launch island, is a barrier island between Pulicat Lake and the Bay of Bengal.
Rameswaram (Pamban) Island lies in the Gulf of Mannar near the Palk Strait.
Munroe Island lies at the confluence of Ashtamudi Lake and the Kallada river, Kerala.
Netrani Island off Murudeshwar, Karnataka, is known for coral and diving.
Viper Island (Andaman) was a British colonial prison site.
Diu island lies off the Kathiawar coast with a Portuguese fort.
Rani Jhansi Marine National Park protects reefs of Ritchie's Archipelago, Andaman.
Lakshadweep sits over the Réunion hotspot volcanic track, capped by coral.
The Thar is also called the Great Indian Desert or Marusthali.
The Thar covers about 2 lakh km², about 85% of it in India (mainly Rajasthan).
The Thar lies north-west of the Aravalli, which form its south-eastern boundary.
Barchans are crescent-shaped dunes formed by wind blowing from one direction.
Annual rainfall in the Thar is below about 150 mm.
The Luni, the Thar's main river, rises in the Aravalli near Ajmer and ends in the Rann of Kutch — an inland/ephemeral river.
Streams of the Thar end in playas (dry salt lake beds, locally dhands) — inland drainage.
Akal Wood Fossil Park near Jaisalmer preserves fossil tree trunks showing the region was once forested/under the sea (Mesozoic).
Khejri (Prosopis cineraria) is the signature tree of the Thar.
The Thar has salt, gypsum, limestone and phosphate; oil is produced near Barmer.
Mushroom rocks and oases (Phalodi, Jaisalmer, Barmer) are Thar landforms.
The area from which a river collects water is its catchment area; a drainage basin is the area drained by a river and its tributaries.
Watersheds are small drainage units and basins large ones; both are treated as planning regions because of their unity.
A rectangular drainage pattern develops on strongly jointed rocky terrain.
A trellis pattern develops where hard and soft rocks lie parallel to each other, with tributaries joining at right angles.
By catchment size: major rivers > 20,000 km², medium 2,000–20,000 km², minor < 2,000 km².
About 77% of India's drainage area goes to the Bay of Bengal and 23% to the Arabian Sea.
The Delhi Ridge, the Aravalli and the Sahyadri form the water divide between Bay of Bengal and Arabian Sea drainage.
Himalayan rivers are antecedent/consequent with dendritic patterns in the plains; Peninsular rivers are superimposed and rejuvenated with trellis, radial and rectangular patterns.
Peninsular rivers are old, with graded profiles near base level and fixed courses; Himalayan rivers are young, eroding headward and shifting course in the plains.
Geologists hold that one Miocene river, the Shiwalik or Indo-Brahma, once flowed from Assam to Punjab and the Gulf of Sindh.
Its break-up followed the Pleistocene uplift of the Potwar plateau (Delhi Ridge), dividing Indus and Ganga systems; the Malda gap turned the Ganga and Brahmaputra to the Bay.
Himalayan rivers cut gorges and V-shaped valleys in the mountains and form meanders, ox-bow lakes, braided channels and deltas in the plains.
Peninsular drainage was shaped by subsidence of the western flank (early Tertiary), Himalayan uplift faulting the northern edge, and a NW–SE tilt of the block.
Peninsular rivers have low gradients, fixed courses, mostly non-perennial flow and broad shallow valleys.
India has 14 major river basins (Central Water Commission classification), 44 medium and many minor basins.
The Indus rises from a glacier near Bokhar Chu in the Kailash range near Mansarovar, Tibet.
In Tibet the Indus is called Singi Khamban (Lion's Mouth).
The Indus enters India (Ladakh) at Demchok and flows between the Ladakh and Karakoram ranges.
The Zanskar joins the Indus near Leh; the Shyok joins it further downstream.
The Panchnad joins the Indus near Mithankot (Pakistan); the Indus enters the Arabian Sea near Karachi.
The Indus is about 3,180 km long (overall).
The blind Indus river dolphin lives only in the Indus.
Left-bank Indus tributaries include the Zanskar, Suru, Soan and the five Punjab rivers; right-bank ones include the Shyok, Gilgit, Hunza, Swat, Kurram, Gomal and Kabul.
The Chenab is formed by the Chandra and Bhaga near Bara-lacha La (as Chandrabhaga) and is the largest Indus tributary.
The Jhelum rises at the Verinag spring in the Kashmir Valley, flows through Wular Lake and joins the Chenab in Pakistan.
The Kishanganga (Neelum) is the largest tributary of the Jhelum.
The Ravi rises in the Kullu hills/Dhauladhar (Chamba) and has the Ranjit Sagar (Thein) dam.
The Sutlej rises near Mansarovar (Rakas Tal), enters India through Shipki La and carries the Bhakra–Nangal project.
The Beas rises at Beas Kund near Rohtang and joins the Sutlej at Harike (Punjab).
The Shyok rises from the Rimo glacier; the Nubra (from the Siachen/Nubra glacier) is its tributary.
The Indus Waters Treaty (1960, brokered by the World Bank) gave India the eastern rivers (Ravi, Beas, Sutlej) and Pakistan the western rivers (Indus, Jhelum, Chenab).
India placed the Indus Waters Treaty "in abeyance" in April 2025 after the Pahalgam terror attack.
The treaty allows India limited non-consumptive uses (such as run-of-river hydropower) on the western rivers.
The Bhagirathi rises at Gaumukh, the snout of the Gangotri glacier (about 3,892 m).
The Alaknanda rises from the Satopanth and Bhagirath Kharak glaciers; Badrinath lies on it.
The Bhagirathi and Alaknanda join at Devprayag to form the Ganga.
At Rudraprayag the Mandakini joins the Alaknanda.
At Nandaprayag the Nandakini joins the Alaknanda.
At Karnaprayag the Pindar joins the Alaknanda.
At Vishnuprayag the Dhauliganga joins the Alaknanda.
The Ganga enters the plains at Haridwar, where the Upper Ganga Canal takes off; Narora feeds the Lower Ganga Canal.
The Ganga is about 2,525 km long and its basin covers about 26.4% of India, home to nearly half its population.
The Ganga mainstream flows through Uttarakhand, Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, Jharkhand and West Bengal.
The Ramganga rises near Dudhatoli (Chamoli), flows through Corbett NP and joins the Ganga near Kannauj.
The Yamuna joins the Ganga at Prayagraj (Allahabad).
The Gomti rises near Pilibhit and joins the Ganga near Ghazipur; the Sai is its tributary.
The Ghaghara (Karnali) rises near Mansarovar, flows through Nepal and joins the Ganga at Chhapra (Bihar).
The Gandak (Kali Gandaki–Trisuli, Nepal) joins the Ganga at Sonepur near Patna.
The Kosi (Saptakoshi, seven streams) is the "Sorrow of Bihar" and joins the Ganga at Kursela.
The Son, the largest south-bank tributary of the Ganga, rises at Amarkantak and joins near Patna.
The Yamuna rises at the Yamunotri glacier on the Bandarpunch; the Tons is its largest Himalayan tributary.
The Chambal, Sind, Betwa and Ken are right-bank tributaries of the Yamuna; the Hindon a left-bank one.
The Farakka Barrage (West Bengal) diverts water through a feeder canal into the Hooghly.
Below Farakka the Ganga splits into the Bhagirathi–Hooghly (right) and the Padma (left), which enters Bangladesh to join the Brahmaputra and Meghna.
The Ganga–Brahmaputra delta is the world's largest delta, covered with mangroves.
The Ganga was declared India's National River in 2008; the Ganges dolphin is the National Aquatic Animal.
The Dhauliganga rises at Vasundhara Tal; the Tapovan–Vishnugad hydro project is on it.
Cities on the Ganga include Rishikesh, Haridwar, Kanpur, Prayagraj, Varanasi, Patna, Bhagalpur and Kolkata (Hooghly).
The Brahmaputra rises from the Chemayungdung glacier in south-west Tibet near the sources of the Indus and Sutlej.
As the Tsangpo ("the Purifier") it flows gently east and is navigable for about 640 km in Tibet.
Names: Yarlung Tsangpo (Tibet), Dihang/Siang (Arunachal), Brahmaputra (Assam), Jamuna (Bangladesh), then Padma–Meghna.
West of Sadiya the Dihang is joined by the Dibang and Lohit and takes the name Brahmaputra.
The Brahmaputra is about 2,900 km long.
The Subansiri ("Gold River", for its gold dust) is a right-bank tributary in Arunachal with a large hydel project.
The Manas rises in Bhutan and joins the Brahmaputra at Jogighopa; Manas NP lies in its valley.
The Teesta rises at Tso Lhamo lake (North Sikkim), receives the Rangeet and joins the Brahmaputra in Bangladesh.
The Kameng rises near Tawang and flows past West Kameng to the Kaziranga area.
The Lohit rises in eastern Tibet and flows through the Mishmi Hills.
The Kopili is the largest south-bank tributary in Assam (Meghalaya–Assam).
The Dhansiri (Nagaland–Assam) is a left-bank (south-bank) tributary.
Right-bank (north) tributaries: Subansiri, Kameng, Manas, Sankosh, Raidak, Jaldhaka, Teesta; left-bank: Lohit, Dibang, Dhansiri, Kolong, Kopili, Burhi Dihing.
Majuli and Umananda in the Brahmaputra are the largest and smallest inhabited river islands.
The Brahmaputra basin spans Arunachal Pradesh, Assam, Meghalaya, Nagaland, Sikkim and West Bengal.
Dibrugarh, Pasighat, Tezpur and Guwahati are cities on the Brahmaputra.
Hydel projects of the Brahmaputra system include Subansiri Lower, Ranganadi and Kameng (Arunachal), Doyang (Nagaland), Loktak (Manipur) and Kopili (Assam).
The Dibang enters the plains of Arunachal near Nizamghat.
The Brahmaputra in Assam is braided, heavily silt-laden and flood-prone.
The Mahanadi rises near Sihawa/Pharsiya in the Dhamtari–Raipur area of Chhattisgarh (Dandakaranya).
The Mahanadi is about 851 km long and second only to the Godavari in water potential among Peninsular rivers.
The Hirakud Dam near Sambalpur forms a 55 km-long lake; the Mahanadi reaches the sea at False Point near Puri after passing Cuttack.
Mahanadi tributaries: Seonath, Hasdeo, Mand, Ib (left) and Ong, Tel, Jonk (right).
The Mahanadi basin hosts Bhilai steel and aluminium at Hirakud and Korba.
The Godavari (about 1,465 km) is the longest Peninsular river and second-longest in India, called Dakshin Ganga or Vriddha Ganga.
The Godavari rises at Trimbakeshwar near Nashik, Maharashtra.
The Godavari basin spans Maharashtra, Telangana, Andhra Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Odisha and small parts of MP, Karnataka and Puducherry (Yanam).
Below Rajahmundry the Godavari splits into the Gautami (east) and Vasishta (west) branches, forming a lobate delta.
The Pranahita, formed by the Wardha, Wainganga and Penganga, is the largest Godavari tributary by catchment.
The Indravati (Odisha–Chhattisgarh, Bastar) is a left-bank Godavari tributary.
The Sabari (Kolab) is a left-bank Godavari tributary from Odisha, joining in Andhra Pradesh.
The Manjira (Balaghat range) is a right-bank Godavari tributary with the Nizam Sagar dam.
Godavari projects include Sriram Sagar (Pochampad), Jaikwadi, the Godavari (Dowleswaram) barrage and Polavaram.
Marathwada in the Godavari basin is drought-prone, while the delta suffers floods and cyclones.
The Krishna rises at Mahabaleshwar (near Jor, Satara) at about 1,300 m and is about 1,400 km long.
The Tungabhadra, formed by the Tunga and Bhadra, is the largest Krishna tributary; Hospet and Kurnool lie on it.
The Koyna (Maharashtra) flows north–south; the Koyna dam is Maharashtra's largest hydel project.
The Bhima rises in the Bhimashankar hills and is a left-bank Krishna tributary (Ujjani dam).
The Musi rises in the Anantagiri hills (Vikarabad) and flows through Hyderabad (Osman Sagar, Himayat Sagar).
The Panchganga (Kolhapur) is formed by four streams — Kasari, Kumbhi, Tulsi and Bhogawati.
Right-bank Krishna tributaries: Venna, Koyna, Panchganga, Dudhganga, Ghataprabha, Malaprabha, Tungabhadra; left-bank: Bhima, Dindi, Musi, Paleru, Munneru.
Krishna dams: Almatti, Srisailam, Nagarjuna Sagar and the Prakasam Barrage at Vijayawada.
Cities on the Krishna include Sangli, Karad, Bagalkot area, Srisailam, Amaravati and Vijayawada.
Rayalaseema and parts of Karnataka and Maharashtra in the Krishna basin are drought-prone.
The Cauvery rises at Talakaveri on the Brahmagiri range (Kodagu, Karnataka) and is about 800 km long.
The Cauvery is called the "Ganga of the South" and its delta the "Garden of Southern India".
The Cauvery is almost perennial because Karnataka gets SW-monsoon rain and Tamil Nadu NE-monsoon rain; 90–95% of its potential is harnessed.
The Cauvery falls at Sivasamudram and splits around Srirangam island; Mekedatu (Goat's Leap) lies on the Karnataka–TN border.
The Kabini (Wayanad, Kerala) is a right-bank Cauvery tributary.
The Hemavati, Harangi, Shimsha and Arkavati are left-bank Cauvery tributaries.
The Bhavani, Noyil and Amaravati are right-bank Cauvery tributaries in Tamil Nadu.
Cauvery dams: Krishnarajasagar (KRS, Karnataka) and Mettur (Tamil Nadu); the Grand Anicut (Kallanai) is in its delta.
The Cauvery dispute between Karnataka and Tamil Nadu goes back to the 1892 and 1924 agreements.
The Damodar rises in the Chotanagpur plateau (Jharkhand), is about 541 km long, joins the Hooghly and was the "Sorrow of Bengal".
The Damodar Valley Corporation (1948), modelled on the Tennessee Valley Authority, built Tilaiya, Konar, Maithon and Panchet dams.
The Barakar is the main tributary of the Damodar (Maithon dam).
The Damodar valley is India's main coal belt — Jharia, Dhanbad ("Coal Capital"), Bokaro and Durgapur steel.
The Subarnarekha ("streak of gold") rises near Nagri (Ranchi), is about 395 km long and passes Jamshedpur; the Kharkai is its tributary.
The Brahmani (Koel + Sankh) and Baitarani rise in the Chotanagpur plateau and form a joint delta with the Mahanadi.
The Penner (Pennar) rises in the Nandi Hills (Karnataka), is about 597 km long and reaches the sea in Nellore district, AP.
Penner tributaries include the Chitravathi, Papagni, Kunderu and Sagileru; the Somasila dam is on it.
The Palar and Vaigai are east-flowing rivers of Tamil Nadu (Vaigai at Madurai).
Peninsular rivers are older than the Himalayan ones, with broad graded valleys; the Western Ghats are their main water divide.
The Narmada rises at Amarkantak (Maikal range, MP), is about 1,312 km long and flows west through a rift valley between the Vindhya and Satpura.
The Narmada forms the Marble Rocks gorge at Bhedaghat and the Dhuandhar falls near Jabalpur.
The Narmada enters the Gulf of Khambhat by an estuary near Bharuch.
Narmada tributaries include the Tawa (largest), Hiran, Banjar, Shakkar, Dudhi and Burhner.
The Tapi rises at Multai (Betul, MP), is about 724 km long, flows through a rift valley south of the Satpura and reaches the sea near Surat (Ukai dam).
Tapi tributaries include the Purna, Girna, Panjhra, Bori and Waghur.
The Mahi (about 583 km) rises in the Vindhya and crosses the Tropic of Cancer twice before entering the Gulf of Khambhat.
The Sabarmati (about 371 km) rises in the Aravalli (Rajasthan) and flows past Ahmedabad.
The Periyar (about 244 km) is Kerala's longest river (Idukki, Mullaperiyar dams).
The Sharavati (Karnataka) forms Jog Falls; the Mandovi and Zuari drain Goa.
The Bharathapuzha (Nila) is Kerala's second-longest river.
The Narmada and Tapi flow west because they occupy fault (rift) troughs formed when the northern Peninsula subsided during the Himalayan uplift.
By quoted length: Indus ~3,180 km, Brahmaputra ~2,900 km, Ganga 2,525 km; the Godavari (1,465 km) is the longest Peninsular river.
The Luni is an inland river of Rajasthan that ends in the Rann of Kutch.
Dal Lake in Srinagar is known for houseboats and shikaras.
Wular Lake (J&K), fed by the Jhelum, is India's largest freshwater lake.
Renuka is the largest natural lake of Himachal Pradesh (a Ramsar site).
Chandratal ("Moon Lake", Lahaul–Spiti) is a crescent-shaped high-altitude lake.
Gobind Sagar is the reservoir of the Bhakra dam on the Sutlej.
Roopkund (Uttarakhand) is the "Skeleton Lake".
Nainital and Bhimtal are natural lakes of the Kumaon hills.
Harike wetland (Punjab) lies at the Beas–Sutlej confluence and is a Ramsar site.
Sukhna Lake in Chandigarh is man-made.
Kodaikanal Lake (Tamil Nadu) is a star-shaped artificial lake.
Ooty Lake is man-made; Veeranam lake supplies water to Chennai.
Vembanad is Kerala's largest lake and India's longest lake, part of the backwaters (Ramsar).
Ashtamudi (Kerala) is a palm-shaped backwater lake.
Sasthamcotta is Kerala's largest freshwater lake.
Kolleru (AP), between the Godavari and Krishna deltas, is one of India's largest natural freshwater lakes (Ramsar).
Pulicat (AP–TN) is India's second-largest brackish-water lagoon, famous for flamingos.
Hussain Sagar in Hyderabad is man-made with a monolithic Buddha statue.
Bhojtal (Upper Lake, Bhopal) was made by Raja Bhoj; with the Lower Lake it forms the Bhoj Wetland.
Kanwar Lake (Bihar) is Asia's largest freshwater oxbow lake.
Chilika (Odisha) is India's largest coastal brackish lagoon, a Ramsar site with Irrawaddy dolphins.
Deepor Beel near Guwahati is a Ramsar freshwater wetland.
Tsomgo (Changu) and Gurudongmar are high glacial lakes of Sikkim.
Loktak (Manipur) is the largest freshwater lake of the north-east, with floating phumdis and Keibul Lamjao NP.
Umiam (Meghalaya) is a reservoir lake on the Umiam river.
Sambhar (Rajasthan) is India's largest inland salt lake.
Didwana, Kuchaman, Sargol and Khatu are saline lakes of Rajasthan.
Pushkar is a sacred lake; Pichola is Udaipur's palace lake; Jaisamand (Dhebar) is India's second-largest artificial lake.
Nal Sarovar and Thol (Gujarat) are bird-sanctuary lakes.
Lonar (Buldhana, Maharashtra) is a saline, alkaline lake in a meteor-impact crater in basalt.
Pangong Tso and Tso Moriri are high-altitude lakes of Ladakh; Pangong straddles the India–China line.
East Kolkata Wetlands are known for sewage-fed fisheries (wastewater recycling).
Carambolim (Goa) is a bird-watching lake.
Kunchikal Falls (Varahi river, Shivamogga, Karnataka; about 455 m) is the highest waterfall in India.
Jog (Gersoppa) Falls on the Sharavati (Karnataka) is a segmented fall of about 253 m with a large volume.
Nohkalikai Falls (East Khasi Hills, Meghalaya) is India's tallest plunge waterfall.
Dudhsagar Falls on the Mandovi lies on the Goa–Karnataka border.
Athirappilly Falls on the Chalakudy (Thrissur, Kerala) is called the "Niagara of India".
Chitrakote Falls on the Indravati (Bastar, Chhattisgarh) is the widest fall, also called the "Niagara of India".
Tirathgarh Falls (Kanger valley, Bastar) is another Chhattisgarh fall.
Shivanasamudra Falls is on the Kaveri (Karnataka); Hogenakkal is on the Kaveri in Tamil Nadu.
Hundru Falls on the Subarnarekha is near Ranchi, Jharkhand.
Dhuandhar Falls on the Narmada is at Bhedaghat near Jabalpur.
Duduma Falls on the Machkund river lies on the Odisha (Koraput)–Andhra Pradesh border.
Talakona Falls (Tirupati district, Sri Venkateswara NP) is the highest waterfall of Andhra Pradesh.
Khandadhar Falls (Sundargarh–Keonjhar) is Odisha's highest; Barehipani is in Similipal.
Lodh Falls (Latehar) is the highest in Jharkhand.
Vantawng Falls (Serchhip) is the highest in Mizoram.
Kakolat Falls is in Nawada district, Bihar.
Rajat Prapat is near Pachmarhi (Satpura), Madhya Pradesh.
Palaruvi Falls on the Kallada is in Kerala.
The Grand Anicut (Kallanai) on the Cauvery, built by Karikala Chola about the 2nd century AD, is India's oldest functioning dam.
Hirakud Dam on the Mahanadi (Odisha) is India's longest dam (about 25.8 km with dykes), a composite earth-fill dam.
Tehri Dam on the Bhagirathi (Uttarakhand) is India's highest dam (about 260.5 m), a rock-and-earth-fill dam.
Bhakra Dam on the Sutlej (HP) is India's highest straight concrete gravity dam (about 226 m); its reservoir is Gobind Sagar.
Nagarjuna Sagar on the Krishna (AP–Telangana) is the world's largest masonry dam.
Sardar Sarovar on the Narmada (Gujarat, about 163 m) is the largest dam of the Narmada Valley Project, benefiting Gujarat, MP, Maharashtra and Rajasthan.
Indira Sagar on the Narmada (MP) has the largest reservoir capacity in India.
Idukki Dam on the Periyar (Kerala) is an arch dam.
Mullaperiyar Dam (1895) on the Periyar is in Kerala but operated by Tamil Nadu — a long dispute.
Pong Dam on the Beas (HP) forms Maharana Pratap Sagar.
Chamera Dam is on the Ravi (HP); Ranjit Sagar (Thein) on the Ravi (Punjab).
Nathpa Jhakri and Kol Dam are on the Sutlej (HP).
Salal and Baglihar are on the Chenab; Uri on the Jhelum; Kishanganga on the Kishanganga (J&K).
Ukai Dam is on the Tapi (Gujarat); Kadana on the Mahi.
Gandhi Sagar (MP), Rana Pratap Sagar and Jawahar Sagar (Rajasthan) are on the Chambal.
Rihand Dam (UP) forms Govind Ballabh Pant Sagar, one of India's largest artificial lakes.
Bansagar Dam is on the Son (MP).
Tungabhadra Dam is at Hospet (Karnataka).
Almatti and Narayanpur (Basava Sagar) dams are on the Krishna in Karnataka.
Krishnarajasagar (KRS) is on the Cauvery near Mysuru; Mettur (Stanley reservoir) on the Cauvery in Tamil Nadu.
Koyna Dam is on the Koyna (Maharashtra); Ujjani on the Bhima.
Maithon (Barakar), Panchet (Damodar), Tilaiya and Konar are DVC dams in Jharkhand.
Rengali Dam is on the Brahmani (Odisha).
Somasila Dam is on the Penner in Andhra Pradesh.
Srisailam Dam is on the Krishna (Nandyal/Kurnool–Telangana border).
Polavaram is a multipurpose national project on the Godavari in Andhra Pradesh.
Sriram Sagar (Pochampad) is on the Godavari; Nizam Sagar and Singur on the Manjira (Telangana).
Dam types: gravity (Bhakra), arch (Idukki), embankment/earth- or rock-fill (Hirakud, Tehri), diversion and storage (Nagarjuna Sagar) dams.
The world's tallest dam is quoted as Nurek (Tajikistan, about 300 m) in our source; the Jawa dam (about 3000 BCE) is among the oldest known.
Monsoons are periodic (secondary) winds that reverse direction with the season — sea to land in summer, land to sea in winter.
A permanent high-pressure cell in the south Indian Ocean (east of Madagascar) plus the Tibetan low drive the SW monsoon.
Onset is controlled by the Subtropical Jet Stream, the Tropical Easterly Jet and the ITCZ; intensity by the Somali (Findlater) jet, Somali current, Walker cell and IOD.
In winter the westerly Subtropical Jet is split by the Himalaya–Tibet; its stronger southern branch (about 240 km/h) blows south of the Himalaya along about 25°N.
In late May–June the southern STJ branch shifts north of the Himalaya and Tibet, allowing the monsoon to burst within days.
The Tropical Easterly Jet (5–20°N, at 6–9 km) blows east to west over the Peninsula from June to early October.
Heavy, widespread snow over Tibet delays heating, weakens the easterly jet and is followed by a weak monsoon.
The Findlater (Somali) current reverses with the monsoon and causes upwelling off the Horn of Africa.
The IOD is the SST difference between a western pole (Arabian Sea) and an eastern pole (south of Indonesia); it peaks around October.
EQUINOO (Equatorial Indian Ocean Oscillation) is the atmospheric component of the IOD.
About 60% of India lies north of the Tropic of Cancer, yet its climate is tropical monsoon type.
The Himalaya block cold Central Asian air, so north India is 3–8°C warmer in winter than places at the same latitude.
The loo is a hot, dry summer wind of the northern plains from the Thar–Baloch–Iranian deserts.
Mawsynram and Cherrapunji (Meghalaya) get about 1,100 cm a year — funnelling plus orographic lift; Jaisalmer rarely gets over 12 cm.
The highest diurnal temperature range is in the Thar; the highest annual range in the Himalaya; coastal ranges are lowest.
The Coromandel coast is dry in July–August (rain shadow of the SW monsoon) and gets its main rain in October–December.
The Arabian Sea branch blows parallel to the Aravalli, so Rajasthan gets little orographic rain (Mount Abu excepted).
Interior Maharashtra, Karnataka, Telangana, AP and TN lie in the rain shadow of the Western Ghats.
Western disturbances from the Mediterranean bring winter rain/snow to the north-west — vital for rabi crops.
Most cyclones form over the Bay of Bengal; Oct–Nov cyclones of the retreating monsoon hit the east coast.
IMD recognises four seasons: cold weather (Dec–Feb), hot weather (Mar–May), SW monsoon (Jun–Sep) and retreating monsoon (Oct–Nov).
Pre-monsoon local storms: mango showers (Kerala–Karnataka), cherry blossom showers (coffee, Karnataka), Kal Baisakhi/Nor'westers (Bengal; "Bardoli Chheerha" in Assam, good for tea and jute).
"October heat" is the hot, humid weather after the monsoon retreats in October.
The SW monsoon normally reaches Kerala around 1 June and covers India by about 8 July (IMD normal).
The Arabian Sea branch is stronger than the Bay of Bengal branch; the Bay branch is deflected west along the Himalaya.
A "break in the monsoon" occurs when the monsoon trough moves to the Himalayan foothills, leaving the plains dry for days.

Köppen climates of India include Amw (short dry season, Konkan/Goa coast), As (dry summer, Coromandel), Aw (tropical savanna), BWhw (hot desert, west Rajasthan), Cwg (Ganga plain) and Dfc/E (Himalaya).
India's average annual rainfall is about 118–125 cm, about 75% of it from the SW monsoon.
Pedology is the study of soils; pedogenesis is soil formation by weathering, leaching and calcification.
Soil formation depends on parent rock, climate, relief, natural vegetation and time.
A soil profile is a vertical section; each layer is a soil horizon.
ICAR classifies Indian soils into eight groups: alluvial, black, red, laterite, forest/mountain, desert, saline-alkaline and peaty/marshy.
Alluvial soil is light to ash grey, sandy loam to clay, rich in potash but poor in phosphorus; sandier in the west.
Black soil is rich in iron, lime, calcium, potash, aluminium and magnesium but poor in nitrogen, phosphorus and organic matter.
Black soil swells and becomes sticky when wet and shrinks with deep cracks when dry ("self-ploughing").
Black soil covers the Deccan lava plateau — Maharashtra, Malwa, Gujarat (Saurashtra), western MP, and parts of Telangana and AP (Godavari–Krishna valleys).
Red soil, called the "omnibus group", forms on crystalline igneous rocks in low rainfall; it is red from ferric oxide and yellow when hydrated.
Red soil is porous and friable, lacks kankar, and is poor in lime, phosphate, nitrogen and humus.
Red soil is widespread in Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, Odisha, Chhattisgarh and Jharkhand.
Laterite takes its name from the Latin "later" (brick); it is soft when wet and hardens on drying, so it is used for bricks.
Laterite forms under high heat and heavy rain by intense leaching of lime and silica; it is rich in iron and aluminium but poor in nitrogen, potash, lime and humus.
Laterite soils suit cashew, tapioca, rubber, tea, coffee, rice and ragi; they occur in Kerala, Karnataka, Tamil Nadu hills, Odisha, Assam and Meghalaya.
Forest and mountain soils (about 8.7% of area) are humus-rich, acidic, silty-loamy and suit tea, coffee and fruits.
Desert soils are wind-laid, sandy, rich in soluble salts, phosphate and calcium but poor in moisture and nitrogen; with irrigation they grow bajra and barley.
Saline-alkaline soils (usar, reh, kallar, thur) occur in western Gujarat, the Sundarbans and over-irrigated Punjab–Haryana; gypsum reclaims them.
Peaty/marshy soils, rich in organic matter, occur in deltas, Kerala (Kuttanad/Alappuzha) and parts of Uttarakhand; they grow rice and jute.
Gully erosion creates ravines (Chambal); sheet erosion strips topsoil evenly; contour ploughing, terracing and shelter belts check erosion.
Alluvial soils grow wheat, rice, maize, sugarcane, pulses and oilseeds.
NCERT groups natural vegetation into tropical evergreen, deciduous (moist and dry), thorn/desert, montane and tidal (mangrove) forests.
Tropical evergreen forests (over 200 cm) grow in the Western Ghats, the north-east, Andamans and Terai, with multi-layered canopies.
Evergreen trees include rosewood, mahogany, ebony, garjan and bamboo.
Moist deciduous forests (100–200 cm) of the eastern Ghats slopes, Chhattisgarh and Odisha have teak, sal, shisham, arjun and mahua.
Dry deciduous forests (70–100 cm) of central India and the Ghats' rain shadow have teak, khair, axlewood, tendu, palash, bel and neem.
Semi-desert/thorn vegetation (under 50 cm) of Gujarat, Rajasthan and Punjab has acacia, babul, khejri and Indian wild date, with long roots and fleshy stems.
Montane forests change with height: sal/teak in the foothills, oak and chestnut, then pine, deodar, fir and spruce, then rhododendron and juniper, then alpine grassland.
Alpine pastures are called bugyals in Uttarakhand and margs (e.g., Gulmarg) in Kashmir.
Mangrove trees include sundari, hogla, garan and pasur.
Mangroves fringe the deltas of the Ganga (Sundarbans), Mahanadi (Bhitarkanika), Godavari–Krishna (Coringa) and Cauvery (Pichavaram).
India's first National Forest Policy was adopted in 1952 and revised in 1988.
The 1988 policy aims at 33% forest/tree cover (two-thirds in the hills), checking soil erosion and desert spread, social forestry and a people's movement with women.
ISFR 2023 (released December 2024): forest cover 21.76% and forest plus tree cover 25.17% of India's area.
By area, Madhya Pradesh has the largest forest cover, followed by Arunachal Pradesh and Chhattisgarh (ISFR 2023).
India's mangrove cover is about 4,992 km² (ISFR 2023), with West Bengal holding the largest share.
Teak is the dominant tree of the deciduous (monsoon) forests, which shed leaves in the dry season.
India has about 45,000 plant species and 91,000 animal species.

Nagarhole (Rajiv Gandhi) National Park is in Karnataka (Kabini forests, tigers).
Bannerghatta National Park is in Karnataka (near Bengaluru).
Kudremukh National Park is in Karnataka (shola grassland, old iron mine).
Anshi National Park is in Karnataka (Kali tiger reserve).
Eravikulam National Park is in Kerala (Nilgiri tahr, Anamudi).
Silent Valley National Park is in Kerala (lion-tailed macaque, Kunthipuzha).
Periyar National Park is in Kerala (elephants around the Thekkady lake).
Mathikettan Shola National Park is in Kerala (shola forest of Idukki).
Mudumalai National Park is in Tamil Nadu (Nilgiri BR elephants and tigers).
Mukurthi National Park is in Tamil Nadu (Nilgiri tahr grasslands).
Indira Gandhi (Anamalai) National Park is in Tamil Nadu (lion-tailed macaque, Anamalai hills).
Gulf of Mannar Marine National Park is in Tamil Nadu (dugong, corals, Balanoglossus).
Guindy National Park is in Tamil Nadu (blackbuck inside Chennai).
Mrugavani National Park is in Telangana (Hyderabad outskirts).
Kasu Brahmananda Reddy National Park is in Telangana (Hyderabad city park).
Papikonda National Park is in Andhra Pradesh (Godavari gorge (2008)).
Sri Venkateswara National Park is in Andhra Pradesh (Tirumala hills, Talakona falls (1989)).
Rajiv Gandhi (Rameswaram) National Park is in Andhra Pradesh (Kadapa district (2005)).
Simlipal National Park is in Odisha (tiger, elephant; biosphere reserve).
Bhitarkanika National Park is in Odisha (saltwater crocodile, second-largest mangrove).

Galathea Bay National Park is in Andaman & Nicobar (leatherback turtle nesting).
Mahatma Gandhi Marine (Wandoor) National Park is in Andaman & Nicobar (corals near Sri Vijaya Puram).
South Button Island National Park is in Andaman & Nicobar (smallest NP of India).
Mount Harriet (Mount Manipur) National Park is in Andaman & Nicobar (renamed Mount Manipur in 2021).
National parks have fixed boundaries, no grazing or private rights, cannot be downgraded to sanctuaries, and their boundaries change only by a resolution of the state legislature.
India has about 106 national parks covering about 1.3% of its area (about 40,500 km²).
Both the Central and State governments can declare national parks.
Sanctuaries and national parks are declared under the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 (our source wrongly says 1947); sanctuaries are IUCN Category IV.
India has about 573 wildlife sanctuaries (Nov 2023) covering about 3.76% of its area.
The largest wildlife sanctuary is the Kutch Desert Wildlife Sanctuary, Gujarat (about 7,506 km²).
Vedanthangal (Tamil Nadu), protected since 1798, is India's oldest bird sanctuary.
Nagarjunasagar–Srisailam (Andhra Pradesh) is India's largest tiger reserve by area (our source wrongly names the Sundarbans).
India had 58 tiger reserves by 2025 — Ratapani (MP) became the 57th and Madhav (MP) the 58th.
Project Tiger (1973) began with 9 reserves; reserves use a core (NP/sanctuary) and buffer (multiple-use) strategy under the statutory NTCA.
The 2022 tiger estimate was at least 3,167 (mean 3,682), about 75% of the world's wild tigers; Madhya Pradesh had the most.
Project Elephant began in February 1992; the elephant was declared the National Heritage Animal in 2010.
The cheetah was declared extinct in India in 1952 and re-introduced at Kuno (MP) from Namibia in September 2022.
The Asiatic lion survives in the wild only in the Gir landscape of Gujarat.
Keoladeo (Bharatpur) is the best-known bird sanctuary, home to over 370 bird species.
Rani Jhansi Marine NP (A&N) is cited as the largest marine sanctuary in our source.
AP sanctuaries in the national list include Coringa, Kolleru, Pulicat (TN side listed), Rollapadu, Nelapattu and Papikonda.
Notable sanctuaries: Udanti (wild buffalo, Chhattisgarh), National Chambal (gharial, MP–UP–Rajasthan), Askot (musk deer, Uttarakhand), Pitti (bird, Lakshadweep).
India has 18 biosphere reserves; 12 were on UNESCO's MAB list by 2020, and the Cold Desert BR became the 13th in 2025.
A biosphere reserve has a core zone (strictly protected), a buffer zone (research, education) and a transition zone (settlements, farming).
Nilgiri (1986, TN–Kerala–Karnataka) was India's first biosphere reserve and the first on the UNESCO list (2000).
Nanda Devi BR (1988) is in Uttarakhand (UNESCO 2004).
Nokrek BR (1988) covers the Garo Hills of Meghalaya (UNESCO 2009).
Great Nicobar BR (1989) is the lowest-lying BR (UNESCO 2013).
Gulf of Mannar BR (1989, Tamil Nadu) is the largest marine BR (UNESCO 2001).
Manas BR (1989) is in Assam.
Sundarban BR (1989) covers the Ganga–Brahmaputra delta, West Bengal (UNESCO 2001).
Simlipal BR (1994) is in Mayurbhanj, Odisha (UNESCO 2009).
Dibru-Saikhowa BR (1997) lies in Dibrugarh–Tinsukia, Assam; the MoEFCC list gives it as the smallest BR (our source names Nokrek).
Dehang-Dibang BR (1998) is in Arunachal Pradesh.
Pachmarhi BR (1999) covers Betul, Hoshangabad and Chhindwara, MP (UNESCO 2009).
Khangchendzonga BR (2000, Sikkim) is the highest BR (UNESCO 2018).
Agasthyamalai BR (2001) spans Tamil Nadu and Kerala (UNESCO 2016).
Achanakmar-Amarkantak BR (2005) spans MP and Chhattisgarh (UNESCO 2012).
Kachchh BR (2008, Gujarat) is the largest BR by area (MoEFCC; our source names Gulf of Mannar).
Cold Desert BR (2009) covers Pin Valley NP, Chandratal and Kibber in Himachal Pradesh.
Seshachalam Hills BR (2010) in the Eastern Ghats of Tirupati–Kadapa (AP) protects red sanders.
Panna BR (2011, MP) was added to the UNESCO list in 2020.
A biosphere reserve protects whole ecosystems with people in its outer zones; a sanctuary mainly protects wild animals.
